subChunks.title: Form Layout and Styling
subChunks.hookHtml: Forms are the most interaction-dense part of any web application. Getting them right means handling inputs, labels, validation states, checkboxes, selects, and error messages — all with proper accessible associations, correct focus indicators, and consistent visual hierarchy. Tailwind has utilities for every piece of this puzzle.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Input anatomy

<div class="flex flex-col gap-1">
  <label class="text-sm font-medium text-gray-700" for="email">Email</label>
  <input
    id="email" type="email"
    class="w-full px-3 py-2 text-sm border border-gray-300 rounded-md
           placeholder:text-gray-400
           focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500 focus:border-blue-500
           disabled:bg-gray-50 disabled:text-gray-500 disabled:cursor-not-allowed"
  />
  <p class="text-xs text-gray-500">We'll never share your email.</p>
</div>

Validation states

/* Error state */
border-red-500 focus:ring-red-500 focus:border-red-500

/* Error message */
<p class="text-xs text-red-600 mt-1">Email is required.</p>

/* Success state */
border-green-500 focus:ring-green-500

Select element

<select class="w-full px-3 py-2 text-sm border border-gray-300 rounded-md bg-white
               focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500 focus:border-blue-500
               appearance-none cursor-pointer">
  <option value="">Select a tier...</option>
  <option value="app">Apprentice</option>
</select>

appearance-none removes the browser's default dropdown arrow so you can add a custom one.

Textarea

<textarea
  class="w-full px-3 py-2 text-sm border border-gray-300 rounded-md resize-none
         focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500
         min-h-[120px]"
  rows="4"
></textarea>

Checkbox and radio

<!-- Accessible checkbox group -->
<label class="flex items-center gap-3 cursor-pointer">
  <input type="checkbox"
    class="w-4 h-4 rounded border-gray-300 text-blue-600
           focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500 cursor-pointer"
  />
  <span class="text-sm text-gray-700">Remember me</span>
</label>

<!-- Radio group -->
<div class="space-y-2">
  <label class="flex items-center gap-3 cursor-pointer">
    <input type="radio" name="plan" value="free"
      class="w-4 h-4 border-gray-300 text-blue-600 focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500"
    />
    <span class="text-sm text-gray-700">Free plan</span>
  </label>
</div>

Form layout patterns

/* Stacked form (mobile-first) */
<form class="space-y-4">

/* Two-column form on desktop */
<div class="grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 gap-4">

/* Inline form (search bar style) */
<form class="flex gap-2">
  <input class="flex-1 ..." />
  <button class="flex-none ...">Submit</button>
</form>

Form fieldset

<fieldset class="border border-gray-200 rounded-lg p-4">
  <legend class="text-sm font-medium text-gray-900 px-2">Notifications</legend>
  <div class="space-y-3">
    <!-- checkboxes -->
  </div>
</fieldset>

Lyra: "Every input must have an associated label — either via for/id or by wrapping the input inside the label. No exceptions. A form that screen readers can't navigate is not a form — it's a guessing game for a quarter of your users."

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: A form that breaks under keyboard navigation or fails to communicate errors clearly is not a form — it's a barrier. Every input needs a label. Every error needs colour AND text. Every required field needs to say so. Build the form right, and the rest of the interface trusts you.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a complete contact form with proper layout and all interactive states:

  • .form-group: flex, flex-col, gap-1
  • .form-label: text-sm, font-medium, text-gray-700
  • .form-input: w-full, px-3, py-2, text-sm, border, border-gray-300, rounded-md, placeholder:text-gray-400, focus:outline-none, focus:ring-2, focus:ring-blue-500, focus:border-blue-500
  • .form-error: text-xs, text-red-600
  • .form-hint: text-xs, text-gray-500

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a registration form from scratch with: a two-column name row (first name, last name), an email input with error state (red border + red error message), a password input with a hint, a select dropdown for country, a checkbox for terms agreement using peer to show a styled label, and a full-width submit button. subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through the anatomy of a well-built form input — what classes are needed for the container, label, input, hint text, and error message? Why is the focus: state pattern different for inputs vs buttons? Explain the appearance-none class and when you need it.

questions.prompt: A select element shows the browser's default dropdown arrow even after styling with Tailwind. Which class removes it so you can add a custom one?
questions.explanation: appearance-none removes the browser's native form control styling, including the default dropdown arrow on select elements. After applying it, you can add a custom SVG arrow with absolute positioning and pointer-events-none.

questions.prompt: A textarea can be resized by dragging its corner, distorting the form layout. Which class prevents this?
questions.explanation: resize-none sets resize: none on the textarea, preventing the user from dragging its resize handle. Tailwind also provides resize-y (allow vertical resize only) and resize-x (horizontal only) if you want partial resize control.

questions.prompt: A form shows validation errors using only red border colour (no error text). A user who is colour-blind cannot distinguish the error from a normal input. What is the accessible fix?
options: Add an error message text in addition to the red border — colour alone is never sufficient to communicate state (WCAG 1.4.1)
Increase the border thickness from 1px to 2px on error inputs
Add a red background (bg-red-50) in addition to the border
Use aria-invalid on the input — screen readers will announce the error automatically
questions.answer: Add an error message text in addition to the red border — colour alone is never sufficient to communicate state (WCAG 1.4.1)
questions.explanation: WCAG 1.4.1 (Use of Color) requires that colour is not the only visual means of conveying information. An error must be communicated through text (error message), not just a colour change. The complete error pattern is: red border + red error message text + aria-describedby linking the input to the error message for screen readers.
